pageNotes.zhs: 自东汉中叶，三公职渐轻而尚书权渐重，尚书既由宫中近侍转为总揽机要，参预外朝政事，则不复理内勤职务。皇帝为制衡枢机、亲裁要务，乃擢宫中近臣，使之评省尚书奏事、协理文书批答，即后世之'门下省'。亦有另设机密之署，以分尚书部分要权，是为后世之'中书省'。
pageNotes.zht: 自東漢中葉，三公職漸輕而尚書權漸重，尚書既由宮中近侍轉為總攬機要，參預外朝政事，則不復理內勤職務。皇帝為制衡樞機、親裁要務，乃擢宮中近臣，使之評省尚書奏事、協理文書批答，即後世之「門下省」。亦有另設機密之署，以分尚書部分要權，是為後世之「中書省」。
pageNotes.en: From the mid-Eastern (Later) Han onward, the authority of the Three Excellencies gradually waned, while that of the Imperial Secretariats steadily increased. Since the Imperial Secretariats shifted from private attendants of the emperor to officials who managed the core affairs of government and participated in outside court politics, they were no longer involved in internal palace duties. To counterbalance this shift of power and to retain direct control over critical decisions, the emperor selected close palace attendants to review memorials submitted by the Imperial Secretariats and to assist in drafting and issuing responses, an arrangement that later evolved into the Chancellery Department. In some cases, separate confidential offices were also established to take over certain key duties from the Imperial Secretariats, laying the foundations for what would later be known as the Palace Secretariat Department.

categoryNotes.zht: 漢時，「門下」本為泛稱，凡宮中執掌內廷勤務之官吏，皆可冠以此名。及至魏晉，其義轉狹，專指禁中殿中近侍之職。
categoryNotes.zhs: 汉时，'门下'本为泛称，凡宫中执掌内廷勤务之官吏，皆可冠以此名。及至魏晋，其义转狭，专指禁中殿中近侍之职。
categoryNotes.en: During the Han, 門下 menxia (“At/Within the Gates”) was originally a broad, generic term, applied to officials responsible for any court duties within the palace. By the Wei-Jin period, however, its meaning had narrowed, referring specifically to close attendants serving in the inner halls of the imperial palace.

categoryNotes.zht: 亦稱門下省。門下即黃門之下，其署設於宮禁中，其官得出入宮禁。高官加門下者，能出入殿省，入宮議政。
categoryNotes.zhs: 亦称门下省。门下即黄门之下，其署设于宫禁中，其官得出入宫禁。高官加门下者，能出入殿省，入宫议政。
categoryNotes.en: Also known as the Chancellery Department, the 門下 (Menxia, literally “At/Within the Gates”) refers to officials historically connected with the 黃門 (Huangmen, “Yellow Gate”). These officials operated within the imperial palace complex and were granted the privilege of entering and exiting the palace freely. High-ranking officals who were conferred additional Chancellery titles were likewise permitted to pass through palace gates and attend imperial halls to participate directly in discussions of state affairs.

categoryNotes.en: Wei had a total of 25 divisions: Palace Affairs, Personnel, Carriage, Finance, Forestry, Judicial Affairs, Southern and Northern Guest, Rituals, Expenditure, Storage, Agriculture, Waterways, Rites, Three Excellencies, Granaries, Civil, Two-thousand shi, Central Troops, External Troops, Capital Troops, Specialized Troops, Merit Assessment, Ordinance, Capital Officials and Cavalry Divisions. The Personnel Section is more prestigious the other Sections, in charge of official selection matters; the Civil Section oversees repairs, construction works, salt fields, and gardens; the Guest Section manages affairs related to foreign states and tribes; the Troop Section was in charge of central troops, external troops, cavalry, specialized troops, and capital troops; the Expenditure Section exclusively manage financial planning for military and state expenditures; additionally, the five Section Imperial Secretaries, two Deputy Directors, and one Director collectively made up the Eight Seats.

categoryNotes.en: In the pre-Qin period, the Censor was originally a court historian responsible for records and archives. From the Qin and Han onward, this office was maintained and further entrusted with the supervision of officials. During the Western (Former) Han, the Imperial Censor ranked just below the Chancellor and functioned as both his collaborator and institutional counterweight. By the Eastern (Later) Han, however, the Imperial Censor title was changed to Excellency of Works among the Three Excellencies, its authority gradually hollowed out, and effective control of the Censorate passed instead to the Deputy Imperial Censor.
